title: Platelet activation and procoagulant platelets in patients with immune thrombocytopenia: a prospective study
summary:
Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) is a blood disorder in which the body’s immune system mistakenly attacks its own platelets, the tiny cells that help stop bleeding. Most research has focused on the low platelet count and the risk of bruising or bleeding. However, recent evidence suggests that some ITP patients may also face an increased risk of blood clots—an unexpected combination of bleeding and clotting.
In this three‑year study, doctors will follow 50 adults with ITP and 15 control patients who have low platelets for other reasons. At the first visit and then every six months, a small blood sample will be taken. Researchers will measure a special “procoagulant” behaviour of platelets and record any bleeding episodes or clotting events such as deep‑vein thrombosis or stroke.
By comparing changes in these pro‑clotting platelets with each person’s bleeding or clotting history, the team hopes to discover why some people with ITP bleed while others clot. The findings could lead to more personalised treatment—helping doctors decide who needs stronger clot‑preventing care and who needs additional support to stop bleeding.

interventions.name: ITP Cohort: The determination of platelet phenotypes by flow cytometry at the first visit and then every six months upto 2 years. Clinical data such as treatment response, bleeding score and thrombotic events will be recorded.
Control group: A control group is formed from patients with thrombocytopenia who do not have ITP. Platelet phenotypes will be determined only at the first visit.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Diagnosis of ITP according to established diagnostic criteria.
Willingness to voluntarily participate in the study and sign the written informed consent form.
Exclusion criteria:
Pregnancy or breastfeeding.
Active infectious diseases or other serious medical conditions that could jeopardise participation in the study.
Presence of other haematological disorders that could affect the interpretation of the results.
